body:
Why industry uses ionising radiation

Radiation can penetrate materials, interact differently with substances of different density or thickness, and be measured using detectors. These properties make it useful for inspecting objects, controlling industrial processes and studying the movement of materials.

Many industrial applications involve sealed radioactive sources, in which the radioactive material is enclosed within a suitable protective capsule. Other applications use electrically generated radiation.

Industrial radiography

Industrial radiography is a form of non-destructive testing (NDT). It uses penetrating radiation to examine the internal condition of an object without cutting it open or destroying it.

For example, a weld may appear sound from the outside but contain internal voids, cracks or other defects. When gamma rays or X-rays pass through the weld and reach a suitable detector, differences in transmitted radiation can help reveal some internal defects.

Iridium-192 and cobalt-60 are radioisotopes used in certain industrial gamma-radiography applications. The appropriate source and method depend on the material and examination requirements.

The detector records information about how much radiation passes through different regions of the object. A defect may change the amount of material along the radiation path, producing a detectable contrast.

Industrial radiography is inspection, not repair. Detecting a defect does not automatically correct it. Radiographic work also requires strict controls because its radiation sources may be hazardous.

Nucleonic gauges

A nucleonic gauge uses radiation to measure or monitor a physical property of a material during an industrial process. Detectors measure radiation transmitted through or scattered by the material.

Examples include:

  • Thickness measurement: monitoring the thickness of paper, plastic film, metal sheet or similar products.
  • Density measurement: monitoring the density of selected materials during processing.
  • Level measurement: detecting the level of material inside a suitable industrial vessel.

The method is useful where an ordinary measuring device may be difficult to place directly inside a moving production line or closed container.

Depending on the application, beta or gamma radiation may be used. Some industrial gauges use radioactive isotopes such as caesium-137 or cobalt-60.

Radiotracers in industry

In a radiotracer study, a small, controlled amount of a radioactive substance is introduced into a system so that its movement can be detected.

For example, investigators may monitor the movement of a tracer through a fluid system to study flow patterns or locate certain leaks. The tracer does not repair the leak; it helps identify where a problem may exist.

Radiotracer techniques can also be used in research on mixing, transport and other industrial processes. Such work requires authorised facilities, suitable isotopes and protection against unintended contamination.

Radiation processing of materials

Radiation can modify the chemical structure of some materials. In selected polymers, controlled irradiation can produce cross-linking, in which molecular chains become connected. This can alter properties such as mechanical strength or resistance to heat.

Other radiation-processing applications include sterilisation of appropriate healthcare products and controlled treatment of industrial materials. The specific result depends on the material and radiation conditions.

Radioisotopes in scientific research

Tracing chemical and biological processes

Radioactive tracers can help researchers follow the movement of substances through biological tissues, chemical reactions, soils and environmental systems. A detector measures the emitted radiation, allowing researchers to study processes that may otherwise be difficult to observe.

Radiocarbon dating

Carbon-14 is a naturally occurring radioactive isotope used in radiocarbon dating. Living organisms exchange carbon with their environment. After an organism dies, this exchange largely stops, while its carbon-14 continues to decay.

By measuring the remaining carbon-14 under appropriate conditions, researchers can estimate the age of once-living materials such as wood, bone or charcoal.

Radiocarbon dating is not a general method for determining the age of every rock or mineral. Its application depends on the presence and preservation of suitable carbon-containing material.

Research reactors and radioisotope production

Some useful radioisotopes are produced by exposing suitable materials to neutrons in research reactors. Others can be produced using particle accelerators. The resulting isotopes may then be prepared for medical, industrial or scientific use.

For example, molybdenum-99 is an important parent radioisotope used to obtain technetium-99m for diagnostic nuclear medicine. This connects research reactor applications with hospital imaging.

Prelims focus

  • Industrial radiography is a non-destructive testing method.
  • Iridium-192 is used for certain weld-radiography applications.
  • Nucleonic gauges can measure thickness, density or level.
  • Radiotracers help study the movement of substances through a system.
  • Carbon-14 dating is primarily associated with suitable once-living material.
  • Trap: A radiotracer follows a process; industrial radiography examines internal structure.

[Sources: International Atomic Energy Agency, Applications of Research Reactors, Nuclear Energy Series No. NP-T-5.3, 2014, sections 5 and 12 and Annex II, printed pp. 92-93; Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, Radiation Applications, industrial radiography, nucleonic gauges and research categories; Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Setting Up of a Gamma Radiation Processing Plant, materials modification applications; consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Industrial and Scientific Uses of Radiation and Radioisotopes

body:
Why radiation protection is necessary

Ionising radiation can damage molecules and living cells. The extent and nature of possible harm depend on factors such as the absorbed dose, radiation type, exposure conditions and affected tissue.

High exposures can cause tissue damage. Lower exposures may increase the probability of certain long-term effects, including cancer. This does not mean that every radiation exposure causes an observable injury. Risks must be understood in relation to the type and amount of exposure.

Because radiation also has important medical, industrial and agricultural benefits, radiation safety aims to ensure that justified applications can take place while unnecessary exposure is prevented or reduced.

Three elementary principles of protection

Time

Reduce unnecessary time spent near a radiation source. Other factors being equal, a shorter period of exposure reduces the accumulated dose.

Distance

Increase the distance from a source where practical. For a small, unshielded point source in suitable conditions, radiation intensity generally decreases approximately according to the inverse square of distance.

For example, increasing the distance from 1 metre to 2 metres from such a source can reduce the radiation intensity to approximately 1-quarter. This simplified relationship does not describe every radiation field or every shielding arrangement.

Shielding

Place suitable material between the source and the person or object requiring protection. The shielding material must suit the type and energy of radiation.

Paper can stop ordinary alpha particles. Suitable plastic is often used for beta radiation. Dense materials such as lead or thick concrete can attenuate gamma rays. Hydrogen-rich materials are useful for slowing neutrons.

Time, distance and shielding are the basic practical methods for reducing external radiation exposure. Their effectiveness depends on the actual source, radiation type and work conditions.

ALARA and justified uses

The ALARA principle means keeping radiation exposures As Low As Reasonably Achievable, taking account of economic and social factors.

Radiation protection also involves deciding whether an activity is justified by its expected benefit. A medically necessary radiological examination may provide important diagnostic information, but an unnecessary exposure should be avoided.

ALARA does not mean that all exposures must be exactly zero. It means keeping exposures as low as reasonably achievable; justification is a separate radiation-protection principle.

Sealed and unsealed sources

A sealed source contains radioactive material within a protective enclosure designed to prevent its normal release. Sealed sources are used in various industrial gauges, radiography equipment and irradiation facilities.

An unsealed source is radioactive material that is not enclosed in this way and may be handled as a liquid, gas or other suitable preparation. Some nuclear medicine tracers are examples.

The main protection concerns can differ. External exposure is especially important for many sealed gamma sources, whereas unsealed radioactive materials also require controls against spills, inhalation, ingestion and contamination.

Monitoring, authorised operation and regulation

Radiation facilities use appropriate instruments to detect or measure radiation. Depending on the work, controls may include source shielding, restricted access, monitoring instruments, personnel dosimeters, warning arrangements and trained operators.

A dosimeter is an instrument or device used to assess radiation dose received by a person. It is a monitoring aid, not a shield that blocks radiation.

In India, the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) regulates specified facilities and activities involving ionising radiation, including medical and industrial applications. Operators must obtain applicable approvals and follow relevant safety requirements.

Only trained and authorised personnel should handle radioactive sources or radiation equipment. An unattended or suspected damaged radioactive source must not be touched or moved by an untrained person; the responsible authorities or designated radiation-safety personnel should be informed.

How the 2 parts of this subtopic are connected

Nuclear fusion concerns releasing energy by joining light nuclei under extreme conditions. Its central questions involve fuel, plasma confinement and the technological feasibility of sustained energy production.

Radiation applications concern using ionising radiation or radioisotopes for a defined purpose. These include studying body functions, treating certain diseases, improving agricultural practices, preserving food, examining industrial materials and conducting scientific research.

The subjects are related through nuclear science, but the technology used for food irradiation or medical diagnosis does not require a working fusion power station. Most established radiation applications use radioactive isotopes, X-ray machines, electron accelerators or other existing sources.

Essential distinctions for objective questions

Pair of conceptsCorrect distinction
Fusion and fissionJoining light nuclei versus splitting heavy nuclei
Tokamak and inertial fusionMagnetic confinement versus rapid fuel compression
ITER and a power stationExperimental fusion research versus electricity supply
Irradiation and contaminationRadiation exposure versus unwanted radioactive material
Diagnostic imaging and therapyObtaining medical information versus treating disease
Mutation breeding and food irradiationCreating heritable variation versus preserving harvested products
Radiography and radiotracingExamining internal structure versus following material movement
Bq, Gy and SvActivity, absorbed dose and biologically weighted dose

The complete subtopic at a glance

Prelims focus

  • ALARA means As Low As Reasonably Achievable.
  • The 3 basic methods of reducing external exposure are time, distance and shielding.
  • A dosimeter measures or assesses dose; it does not shield the wearer.
  • AERB regulates specified radiation applications and facilities in India.
  • Fusion experiments and established radiation-processing applications are different technologies.
  • Trap: The ability to use radiation in medicine, agriculture or industry does not depend on commercial fusion electricity becoming available.

[Sources: International Atomic Energy Agency, Radiation Protection and Safety of Radiation Sources: International Basic Safety Standards, sections on protection principles and radiation quantities; International Atomic Energy Agency, Identification of Radioactive Sources and Devices, definitions of sealed sources, irradiation and contamination; Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, Radiation Applications and regulatory approvals for radiation facilities; ITER Organization, Frequently Asked Questions and What Will ITER Do?; consulted 16 November 2026.]
